title: How to Say "Not Yet" to a Release Without Becoming the Blocker
summary: A good "not yet" names what's missing, who owns it and when you'll decide again. How to pause a release with evidence, and the options between shipping and waiting.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Thursday, 4 p.m., release review. The feature looks close. The demo worked twice, the happy path is clean and the PM already has the announcement drafted. One engineer keeps glancing between the release checklist and last week's support tickets. Nobody wants to be the person who slows the room down. Then they say it anyway: "I don't think we're ready. Not yet."

What happens next depends mostly on how that sentence is built. A vague "not yet" sounds like nerves and gets steamrolled. Or worse, it wins, and nobody knows what would change the answer. A specific one gives the room something to work with. This post is about the second kind.

A good "not yet" comes with a path back to yes

Compare two ways of raising the same worry in the release channel:

Vague Specific
"I have a bad feeling about the migration." "The migration hasn't run against a production-sized copy yet, and it touches our biggest table."
"Rollback seems risky." "Nobody has tested a rollback for this schema change. I can try one on staging by tomorrow noon."
"Permissions might be off." "Nobody owns the case where a view-only user opens a shared link. Can Product decide the expected behavior today?"
"We won't know if it breaks." "The checkout dashboard doesn't track the new flow yet. If it fails, support will hear about it before we do."

Every line on the right names the missing piece and hints at who can close it. That's what makes caution easy to respect: a short list of things that would change the answer. A useful "not yet" has four parts:

  • What's missing: the check, test or decision that isn't done.
  • Who owns it: a name or a role, never "someone should".
  • When you'll decide again: "tomorrow at 11" beats "later".
  • What turns it into a yes: a condition anyone can verify.

In the channel, that can be five lines:

Not yet for the export release.
Missing: rollback for the schema change is untested.
Owner: backend on-call, on staging.
Next decision: Friday 11:00, in this channel.
Yes when: rollback runs clean on staging and the export dashboard tracks the new flow.

Agree on the stop rules before you need them

"Not yet" turns personal when it's one engineer's gut against a roadmap. It's far easier when the team agreed on the rules before anyone was under pressure.

Google's SRE teams do this with error budgets. Their example policy is direct: if a service has exceeded its error budget for the preceding four-week window, "we will halt all changes and releases other than P0 issues or security fixes until the service is back within its SLO." The stated goals are to protect customers from repeated SLO misses and to give teams an incentive to balance reliability with new features. Disagreements about the calculation go to the CTO (The Site Reliability Workbook, Error Budget Policy). Nobody has to win an argument in the release meeting, because the policy said no in advance.

Manufacturing worked this out long ago. In the Toyota Production System, jidoka means stopping immediately when an abnormality is detected, so defective products don't keep coming down the line. An operator "can stop the line by pulling the stop cord themselves" (Toyota Production System). The lesson for software teams: stopping is part of the system, and whoever sees the problem gets to pull the cord.

You don't need Google-scale SLOs to borrow the idea. A one-page release checklist the team wrote together does a lot of the work. Google's launch checklist asks things like "Are you storing persistent data?" (then make sure you have backups) and "Do you have any single points of failure in your design?" (SRE book, Reliable Product Launches at Scale). Yours can be five lines. What matters is that it existed before the deadline did.

Between "ship" and "wait" there's a lot of room

"Not yet" rarely has to mean "nothing ships". Most of the time a smaller yes is available:

  • Cut scope. Ship the part that's ready and hold the risky path for the next release.
  • Ship it dark behind a flag. In his article on feature toggles, Pete Hodgson describes release toggles as the most common way to separate feature release from code deployment: the code goes to production, the feature stays off until it's ready (Feature Toggles).
  • Roll out gradually. Google's launch chapter describes moving to a limited group of users, usually between 1 and 10 percent, with each change revertible on its own if something goes wrong.
  • Wait a day. Sometimes the unknown really is too big, and one more day buys the test that matters.

Each option deserves a reason someone else can check. A healthy engineering culture doesn't reward delay. It rewards clear judgment, and some days clear judgment says ship it today.

"Not yet" is what gives "yes" its weight

If a team says yes to everything, yes stops meaning much. Commitments turn into optimism. When the team will pause for specific reasons, its later yes carries weight. Product can plan around it, support can prepare for it and engineering can stand behind it without pretending the risk vanished.

Most of the work behind a good "not yet" is boring: one more test, a look at the logs, a migration note, a message to support asking what wording customers will see. It rarely looks heroic. Mostly it stops a small, avoidable mess from turning into someone else's 2 a.m. page.

There's a cost, and it's fair to name it. A pause can disappoint people who worked hard to get close, and it can expose planning pressure nobody wanted to say out loud. That's why tone matters. The goal is to put the remaining risk on the table clearly enough that the group can decide together, so nobody has to win anything. And once the condition is met, say "OK, ship it" just as clearly as you said "not yet". Raising risk early in general gets its own post: Why Good Teams Surface Risk Early.

Try this week

  • Write your team's release stop rules on one page: what blocks a release, who can call it and how to escalate.
  • Next time you have doubts, use the four-part message: what's missing, who owns it, when you'll decide again and what makes it a yes.
  • Before you say "wait", check whether a flag, a smaller scope or a gradual rollout gets you a safe yes today.
  • When someone pauses a release for a good reason, thank them in the channel.

faqs.q: When should an engineer say "not yet" to a release?
faqs.a: When a specific, checkable risk is still open: a migration never run on realistic data, no tested rollback, an edge case nobody owns, or no monitoring on the new path. A bad feeling is a reason to look closer. Name what's missing before you ask the team to wait.

faqs.q: How do I say "not yet" without being seen as a blocker?
faqs.a: Give four things: what's missing, who owns it, when the team will decide again, and the condition that turns the answer into yes. Offer a smaller option where you can, such as shipping behind a flag or cutting scope, and say yes clearly once the condition is met.

faqs.q: What is an error budget policy?
faqs.a: A rule agreed in advance about what happens when a service has been less reliable than its target. In Google's SRE workbook example, if a service exceeds its error budget over the previous four weeks, the team halts changes and releases except P0 issues and security fixes until it's back within its SLO.

faqs.q: What are the alternatives to delaying a release?
faqs.a: Cut scope and ship the ready part, ship the code dark behind a release toggle, or roll out gradually to a limited group of users (Google describes 1 to 10 percent) with changes you can revert one by one. Waiting a day is still an option when the unknown is too big.

faqs.q: Who should be allowed to pause a release?
faqs.a: Anyone who sees a concrete risk, the same way any operator on a Toyota line can pull the stop cord. Agree on the stop rules and the escalation path beforehand, so a pause is about the checklist and nobody has to argue from rank.
